Prioritization Analysis for Argentina - Visualizer User Guide Inicio In this manual, you will find the description of the usage and operation of the main tools of the map viewer, as well as the technical information of the base layers, the methodology of the prioritization analysis, and the resulting products.

1 Introduction

1 Introduction The viewer is developed as an interactive application that allows the dynamic and simultaneous representation of the products created in this project, along with other reference layers and geographic information elements. This enables an intuitive analysis of spatial data for decision-makers. Due to the large volume of information and the requirement for agile functionality of this tool, data storage is done locally. This visualization application is shared and distributed along with the information layers and this user manual as a standalone desktop application that can be run on either a Windows or Linux system (in the case of Linux, the installation of the R language is required, see Section 3.3). The main features are: Structural design programmed in the R language, one of the most widely used for data analysis. The calculations of the models associated with the prioritization analysis (sequential optimizations) are not executed in real-time. This application allows the visualization of all pre-processed products in an intuitive manner, without the need for specific knowledge of a conventional Geographic Information System (GIS). The data and layers are available locally, which makes the interface’s operation smoother. An internet connection is only required to add reference labels, additional boundaries, and satellite images.

3 Execution and Configuration 3.1 Execution on Windows The viewer is distributed in a compressed file (.zip) that includes the data, executables and documentation. Figure 3.1: File structure. After unzipping, double-click on run visualizer.bat will start the visualizer. To run it, unzip the file “visualizer_windows.zip” and double-click on “run_visualizer.bat”. The execution opens a command window and switches to the system’s default browser. After use, close the browser tab and the command window. 3.2 Configuration The language and resolution can be configured by editing the “config.dat” file. Figure 3.2: The language is selected typing english or espanol. The recommended resolution is either 1920x1080 or auto. 3.3 Installation and Execution for Linux Systems On Linux systems, prior installation of the R language is required (r-base package on Ubuntu/Debian). After unzipping the .zip file, it can be executed by double-clicking on “run_visualizer.sh” and then clicking “Run in Terminal”. Figure 3.3: Excecution under Linux. During the first execution, the required libraries will be installed, so an internet connection is required. This process may take a few minutes.

4 Description of Base Information 4.1 Study Area and Planning Units 4.2 Protected Areas 4.3 Urban Areas 4.4 Biomass Carbon Map 4.5 Clean Water Provision 4.6 Biodiversity Data 4.7 Ecoregions 4.8 Land Use and Land Cover

4 Description of Base Information 4.1 Study Area and Planning Units The study area encompasses the entire continental surface of the Argentine Republic, including the province of Tierra del Fuego. The Malvinas Islands, Isla de los Estados, the South Atlantic Islands, and the Argentine Antarctic Territory are excluded from the analysis. As a result, the considered surface area is 2,780,050 km². The mentioned area is converted into a raster layer, with a POSGAR 2007 projection, and a spatial resolution of 2 km. This results in 693,594 cells of approximately 4 km² each. Each cell is used as a Planning Unit (PU). 4.2 Protected Areas The available database of Protected Areas at the national level (Administración de Parques Nacionales) is used, including national and provincial protected areas equivalent to categories I to VI in the World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA). These areas were projected onto the PU raster for analysis, including all polygons from the database and discarding overlaps. Areas categorized as ‘proposed’, ‘not applicable’, ‘not reported’, and biosphere reserves were excluded. In this way, 71,236 PUs belonging to the current network of protected areas were identified, representing 10.2% of the study area. 4.3 Urban Areas Urban areas with high-intensity use are excluded from the prioritization analysis as they are not suitable for conservation management. To identify these areas, the Human Footprint Factor (Venter 2016) is used. Those PUs with a human footprint factor greater than 25% (the threshold for distinguishing cities, highways, and main roads) are considered urban areas unsuitable for inclusion among priority conservation areas. Using this method, 9,601 PUs were identified as urban areas. 4.4 Biomass Carbon Map The amount of biomass is estimated from land cover maps (MapBiomas 2024) to identify forests, grasslands, and agricultural areas. The biomass content of each class is further adjusted according to biomass tables by climatic zone (Buchhorn 2019). Belowground carbon is estimated from aboveground biomass and root-to-shoot ratios obtained from the Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (IPCC 2019). 4.5 Clean Water Provision To identify areas of greatest relevance for clean water provision in Argentina, the Relative Raw Water Provision Service (RRWPS) index for human consumption is used, following the Co$tingNature methodology (M. Mulligan 2015). This is an index that measures the volume of clean water (unimpacted by humans) available for downstream beneficiaries. The amount of water in each PU is derived from the water balance (precipitation minus actual evapotranspiration) accumulated downstream. The potential water provision services for each PU are first calculated as the volume of clean water available from upstream. The human impact on water quality is quantified using the Human Footprint on Water Quality (HFWQ) index (Mulligan 2011). The potential water service volume is calculated as accumulated precipitation downstream minus actual evapotranspiration. The raw water service depends on the intensity of downstream use, measured as the normalized area of irrigation, the number of people, and the number of dams downstream. Therefore, the RRWPS is the product of the potential service and normalized downstream beneficiaries. The RRWPS is high where the prevailing climate and land use generate large volumes of clean water that can be used (and reused) by a large number of beneficiaries. Not all water provides a service, only that which is used by people or dams. 4.6 Biodiversity Data The best available and taxonomically updated data on species distribution in Argentina are used. These data included all threatened terrestrial mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians present in Argentina. Marine mammals (Pinnipedia and Cetacea) were not included. We collected information on species distribution from two sources: distribution maps and point records. For reptiles and amphibians, distribution maps (or species range maps) were downloaded from the IUCN Red List database (IUCN 2019) and corrected based on expert opinion and collection data, while their conservation status was obtained from national assessments. For mammals, distribution maps were obtained from the National Red List (SAREM 2019). For birds, distribution maps were first obtained from Birdlife International and the Aves Argentinas database eBird Argentina. A reclassification of the threat status was carried out, reviewing the categories assigned by the IUCN Red List (IUCN 2019) and adopting national criteria when deemed appropriate (e.g., species classified as Least Concern by the IUCN but with small populations or marginal distributions in Argentina). In total, 350 species of threatened tetrapods inhabiting Argentina were analyzed in this study (Section 9). The geographic range of species varies in precision, so the range of each species was refined, from the Extent of Occurrence (EOO) to an adjusted range. Land cover maps (MapBiomas 2024) were used to remove from the original EOO habitats that experts considered unlikely for the species. 4.7 Ecoregions Argentina has 15 terrestrial ecoregions that can be viewed in the viewer (Morello 2012). This information is used to divide the ranges of species that extend across more than one ecoregion. The resulting intersections are considered individually with their own conservation target. For example, the distribution range of the Ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) spans four ecoregions: Dry Chaco, Humid Chaco, Yungas, and Paraná Forest. Since this species is nationally classified as Vulnerable, the conservation target is 80% of its range, but instead of applying it to the total range, it is applied by ecoregion, i.e., the target is to protect 80% of the Ocelot’s range in the Dry Chaco, 80% of its range in the Humid Chaco, etc. In this way, intraspecific variation is captured, and the role of the species in each of the ecosystems it inhabits is preserved. By applying this separation into sub-ranges by ecoregion, the number of ranges increases from 350 to 621 sub-ranges with individualized targets. 4.8 Land Use and Land Cover To classify the dominant land use and land cover type in each PU, the MapBiomas Argentina classification (MapBiomas 2024) is used. The annual land cover and land use maps of MapBiomas Argentina are produced from pixel-by-pixel classification of Landsat satellite images. The entire process is carried out on the Google Earth Engine platform. The resulting maps have a resolution of 30 m x 30 m. In the viewer, the dominant cover (i.e., the most frequent) in each 2 km x 2 km PU is displayed.

5 Methodology 5.1 Prioritization Analysis 5.2 Definition of Conservation Targets 5.3 Formulation of the Optimization Problem and Priority Levels 5.4 Prioritization Analysis Variants 5.5 Interaction with Productive Areas

5 Methodology 5.1 Prioritization Analysis The determination of priority areas for biodiversity, carbon and water conservation (or a combination of these objectives) is carried out using systematic conservation planning (SCP) techniques (Kukkala and Moilanen 2013). The study area (continental Argentina) is divided into Planning Units (PUs) with a resolution of 2 km (see Section 4.1 for more details). In each PU, the content of each conservation “feature” (habitat area for each species, tons of biomass carbon, and average value of the water provision index, etc.) is calculated. This procedure includes PUs that are part of the current protected area system, so the contribution of these areas to meeting conservation targets is considered in all analysis variants. The prioritization analysis requires a clear and appropriate definition of conservation targets for each feature (Section 5.2), from which it is possible to evaluate the level of target fulfillment for any set of PUs. The optimization problem consists of finding the combination of PUs that, when added to the current protected areas, maximize the fulfillment of the selected feature’s (or combination of features’) targets (Section 5.3). Through a sequence of optimizations using a 5% area constraint, priority ranges are constructed for the different analysis variants (Section 5.4). Finally, the optimization problem formulation is modified to include an additional cost for selecting PUs containing agricultural or livestock production, aiming to achieve a good balance between land management for conservation and food production (Section 5.5). 5.2 Definition of Conservation Targets Conservation targets for biodiversity are established in terms of the minimum amount of habitat required for each species to reach the “Least Concern” (LC) conservation status, according to IUCN criteria (Mogg 2019). Following the criteria of the most recent SCP work (Jung 2021), the conservation target based on the Area of Habitat (AOH) for species s is defined as, \[Ts = min(max(2200, 0.8*AOH_{s(VU)} ),834000),\] for all species with a “Vulnerable” (VU) conservation status following IUCN Red List Criterion A, which states that the population should not decrease by more than 30% in 10 years, which can be translated into an approximate area-based criterion of 80% of the range (Mogg 2019). For species with “Endangered” (EN) or “Critically Endangered” (CR) status, this fraction is increased from 80% to 100%, i.e., \[Ts = min(max(2200, AOH_{s(EN,CR)} ),834000).\] All values are expressed in km². The AOH value results from the species’ distribution range filtered by suitable habitats and divided by ecoregion to preserve intraspecific variation (see Section 4.6). The AOH values for each species are detailed in the table in Section 9. The Ts values are capped at a maximum of 834,000 km², representing 30% of the continental territory, which is the maximum expansion of protected areas considered in this study. On the other hand, the lower limit for all AOHs is set at 2,000 km² plus a 10% buffer, following IUCN Red List Criterion B2 (IUCN 2012). The targets for biomass carbon and water provision were set at 100% of the total amount of each attribute integrated across the entire study area (Jung 2021). 5.3 Formulation of the Optimization Problem and Priority Levels The assignment of priority levels is carried out through a sequence of optimization problems (Jung 2021). For each conservation feature j (each species, carbon, water, etc.), the goal is to maximize the fulfillment of its conservation target \(T_j\), for which the relative target fulfillment for each feature j is defined as \[z_j = \min \big( 1 , \sum_i^{N_{PU}} R_{ij} x_i / T_j \big)\] where \(R_{ij}\) represents the amount of conservation feature \(j\) contained in PU \(i\) (suitable habitat area, tons of carbon, m³ of water provision, etc.). \(x_i\) is defined as a binary decision variable indicating whether the i-th PU is managed for conservation (value 1) or not (value 0). The value of \(z_j\) is limited to avoid overrepresentation of a conservation feature. To define the objective function to be maximized, weights \(w_j\) are assigned to each conservation feature \(j\), which multiply the target fulfillment to regulate the relative importance of each aspect in the different analysis variants. The optimization problem consists of determining the set of PUs that maximize, \[F_{obj}(x_i) = \sum_j^{N_f} w_j z_j(x_i),\] Subject to the following constraints, \(\sum_i a_i x_i < 0.05 A\), \(x_i = 1\) for all PUs within current protected areas and those selected in the previous prioritization level (from the second execution onward), \(x_i = 0\) for all PUs in urban areas, where \(N_f\) is the number of conservation features considered, \(a_i\) is the area of each PU, and \(A\) is the total area of the study area (both in km²). Current protected areas are included in all considered solutions (“lock-in” constraint). The sequential application of this optimization problem allows identifying the distribution of areas that compose each priority level. For convenience in visualization and presentation of results, four priority levels were set, each covering 5% of the territory. In the first optimization execution, the 5% of the area with the highest priority for the selected conservation analysis variant (the analysis variants are described in Section 5.4) is found, which, together with the 10% of protected areas (actually 10.2%, but rounded for simplicity), covers 15% of the territory. The next level is obtained by solving the optimization problem for an additional 5%, imposing the constraint that the PUs of protected areas and those of the first priority level are part of the solution. The new 5% found represents the second priority level and, together with the protected areas and the previous level, completes 20% of the territory. The same process is repeated to find the third and fourth priority levels, totaling an expansion from 10% to 30% that maximizes the fulfillment of targets for the selected prioritization variant. This general procedure is the same for all prioritization analysis variants detailed in the following section. 5.4 Prioritization Analysis Variants The different analysis variants are obtained by imposing different distributions of relative weights (\(w_j\)) among the conservation features. Table 5.1 shows the prioritization analysis variants available in the viewer with their respective weight distributions. \[ \begin{matrix} \begin{array}{c|l|l} \text{Case} & \text{Analysis Variants} & \text{Weight Distribution} \\\hline 1 & \text{Biomass Carbon} & w_C = 1 \text{, the rest } 0 \\ 2 & \text{Water Provision} & w_{Wat} = 1 \text{, the rest } 0 \\ 3 & \text{Biodiversity} & w_s = SCV_s, w_C = w_{Wat} = 0 \\ 4 & \text{Mammals} & w_s = SCV_s \text{ for mammals, the rest } 0 \\ 5 & \text{Birds} & w_s = SCV_s \text{ for birds, the rest } 0 \\ 6 & \text{Reptiles and Amphibians} & w_s = SCV_s \text{ for reptiles and amphibians, the rest } 0 \\ 7 & \text{Carbon and Biodiversity} & w_C = 1, w_s = SCV_s/\sum_s SCV_s, w_{Wat} = 0 \\ 8 & \text{Carbon and Water} & w_C = w_{Wat} = 1 \text{ and } w_s = 0 \\ 9 & \text{Joint Targets} & w_C = 1, w_{Wat} = 1 , w_s = SCV_s/\sum_s SCV_s \end{array} \end{matrix} \] Table 5.1 : Weight distribution in the optimization for all considered analysis variants The first two analysis variants in the viewer are single-objective prioritizations (carbon and water, respectively). In these cases, only one component of the weight distribution vector will be non-zero, \(w_C\) for carbon and \(w_{Wat}\) for water, and the optimization result will be the areas that maximize the conservation of one of these two objectives. If the goal is to maximize the conservation of carbon and water sources simultaneously, a weight of 1 is assigned to both carbon (\(w_C\)) and water (\(w_{Wat}\)), and zero to the rest (variant 8 in Table 5.1). In the case of biodiversity, the weight for each species is the Species Conservation Value (SCV), which takes into account conservation status, taxonomic uniqueness, and chorotype (Martin 2021). The values assigned to each species are detailed in the table in Section 9. When analyzing priority areas for a specific class (mammals, birds, or herpetofauna), only the SCVs for the species in that class are assigned weights, while the rest are set to zero. When combining biodiversity conservation targets with others, such as carbon, the weight distribution for species must be relativized to the total value (sum of all SCVs), so that the sum of weights assigned to all species equals 1. In this way, biodiversity has the same weight as the other conservation features (Jung 2021). This applies when the conservation objective is multiple and includes biodiversity, cases 7 and 9 in Table 5.1. 5.5 Interaction with Productive Areas The maps that maximize the fulfillment of conservation targets involve varying degrees of overlap with productive lands (crops, livestock, forest plantations, etc.). If the overlap is too large, the conservation solution may become too costly to be effectively implemented. This section describes the model adopted to find alternative solutions that maintain a high level of conservation target fulfillment but have a progressively lower degree of overlap with productive lands, and are therefore easier to implement. For this analysis, only the interaction of productive areas with the resulting distribution from the joint target prioritization (biodiversity, carbon, and water, case 9 in Table 5.1) is considered, including current protected areas and the four priority levels (30% of the territory in total). To find alternative solutions with high conservation values but less interaction with productive areas, the objective function in the optimization problem is modified as follows, \[F_{obj}(x_i) = \sum_j^{N_f} w_j z_j(x_i) - C (\lambda - 1) \sum_i^{N_{PU}} f_{prod,i} x_i,\] where \(f_{prod,i}\) represents the fraction of the area of the i-th PU that has some type of productive cover (crops, livestock, forest plantations, agricultural mosaic), \(\lambda\) is a free parameter ranging from 1 to 5 and interpreted as the relative cost between productive and non-productive land. This value can be controlled with a slider in the viewer. It is an arbitrary and constant value for the entire territory, with the sole purpose of finding new conservation solutions with high levels of target fulfillment and less interaction with productive lands. Note that when \(\lambda=1\), productive and non-productive land become indistinguishable for this objective function, and the previous solution is recovered exactly. Finally, the calibration constant \(C\) is used to balance the relative weight between the two terms of the objective function. For this analysis, it was set at \(10^{-3}\). The second summation in the new objective function represents the overlap of the priority area network with productive areas. Therefore, it is clear that as \(\lambda\) increases, the priority area network found has a lower degree of interaction with productive areas. In addition to the aggregate values of overlap and target fulfillment (shown in a graph), the spatial distribution of overlap with productive areas and the difference in the new solution (with \(\lambda>1\)) compared to the original solution (\(\lambda=1\)) can be viewed in the viewer.

6 Prioritization Maps Following the methodology detailed in Section 5, prioritization maps are obtained for all analysis variants listed in Table 5.1 of Section 5.4. This section summarizes the information provided by each of the obtained maps. 6.1 Biomass Carbon The map obtained through this analysis variant indicates the areas that maximize carbon stock, including aboveground live wood plus roots, litter, and dead wood. For this conservation objective, the target is set at 100% of the total stock. As expected, the distribution of these areas largely coincides with the current distribution of forests. Considering the 4 priority levels (20% of the territory) plus the current protected areas (10%), it is possible to achieve protection of 80% of the biomass carbon stock. 6.2 Water Provision This map indicates the areas that maximize the provision of clean water that can be effectively captured and used for direct human consumption, irrigation, or dams. For this conservation objective, the target is set at 100% of the existing production zones. It is observed that by optimally allocating 20% of the territory, in addition to the 10% of current protected areas, it is possible to achieve protection of 95% of the usable clean water provision. 6.3 Biodiversity This map is obtained by assigning each species its conservation value as a weight in the objective function to be maximized (Section 5.4). The distribution of areas obtained is the one that maximizes the fulfillment of conservation targets for the 350 threatened tetrapod species. The conservation targets are detailed in Section 5.2. The average target fulfillment for biodiversity grows rapidly in this analysis variant. The prioritization results show that the areas with the highest priority level (5% of the territory) can double the level of target fulfillment compared to the current protected areas. 6.4 Mammals This map indicates the areas that maximize the fulfillment of conservation targets for the 131 mammal species with some degree of threat in Argentina. By focusing conservation efforts on threatened mammal species, a rapid increase in target fulfillment is achieved. In particular, the level of target fulfillment of the current protected area system is close to 25%, using 10% of the country’s surface. This value can be increased to almost 70% by adding 5% of the territory. On the other hand, the co-benefits of mammal prioritization are high for Biomass Carbon (due to the importance of forests) and for birds, but relatively low for reptiles and amphibians and water provision. 6.5 Birds This map indicates the areas that maximize the fulfillment of conservation targets for the 91 bird species with some degree of threat in Argentina. The protection of birds can be significantly increased if the area dedicated to conservation is increased from the 10% of the current protected area system to 15%. The protection of birds in Argentina shows a high co-benefit for threatened reptile and amphibian species, but very low for the other conservation aspects considered. 6.6 Reptiles and Amphibians This map indicates the areas that maximize the fulfillment of conservation targets for the 89 reptile and 39 amphibian species with some degree of threat in Argentina. Most reptiles and amphibians have relatively small distribution ranges, allowing a high level of protection with little area dedicated to conservation. In particular, it is possible to achieve 85% of the targets by dedicating an additional 5% to the current protected area system if conservation is prioritized solely for these species. However, the co-benefits with the other conservation aspects are relatively low, as a significant decrease in average target fulfillment is observed (black line compared to the dashed line in the graph above). 6.7 Carbon and Biodiversity This map indicates the areas that maximize biomass carbon stock while simultaneously achieving biodiversity targets. The highest priority areas in this map are of primary interest for carbon markets and also harbor high potential for the conservation of threatened species. To obtain this map, the weighted sum of carbon and biodiversity target fulfillments is imposed as the objective function in the optimizer (Section 5.4). 6.8 Carbon and Water This map indicates the areas that maximize carbon stock while simultaneously identifying areas where water is produced that can be used for human consumption without passing through contamination sources. To obtain this map, the weighted sum of carbon and water provision target fulfillments is imposed as the objective function in the optimizer (Section 5.4). 6.9 Joint Targets This map indicates the distribution of areas that simultaneously maximizes the fulfillment of biodiversity conservation targets, biomass carbon stock, and clean water provision. The results of this analysis variant show that it is possible to increase the fulfillment of targets for these three conservation features simultaneously. In particular, it is observed that it is possible to increase biodiversity and water provision target fulfillment above 80% while biomass carbon stock protection exceeds 60%, optimally extending the current protected areas to cover 30% of the territory. This application allows visualizing all priority levels, indicating the target fulfillment for each conservation feature. 6.10 Interaction with Productive Areas The maps that maximize the fulfillment of conservation targets involve varying degrees of overlap with productive lands (crops, livestock, forest plantations, etc.). If the overlap is too large, the conservation solution may become too costly to be effectively implemented. To find alternative solutions with high conservation values but less interaction with productive areas, a variable factor (adjustable with the slider) is introduced into the optimizer’s objective function, controlling the cost of productive zones relative to land outside the productive framework. See Section 5.5 for more details. When the relative cost is one, planning units with or without production are valued equally by the optimization algorithm, so the same joint target prioritization (biodiversity - carbon - water) at 30% is recovered. As the relative cost of productive areas increases, the optimal solution progressively includes a smaller fraction of these types of lands, and the levels of target fulfillment are modified. In this analysis, the optimization criterion is the maximization of joint targets (biodiversity - carbon - water) over 30% of the territory. 6.10.1 Overlap Map In addition to the modified priority area map due to the increased relative cost of productive areas, an overlap map between productive areas and each conservation solution can be viewed. To see this map, select the “Overlap” button below the cost slider. This layer shows three levels of overlap between priority conservation areas and productive zones. This overlap decreases as the relative cost of productive areas increases. 6.10.2 Difference Map with Original Solution By selecting the “Difference with original solution” button, the subtraction between the solution considering the additional cost of productive zones and the original prioritization is visualized. As a result, -1 is obtained in the areas of the original solution that had high overlap with productive lands, 1 in the areas of the new solution with less overlap, and 0 in the areas common to both solutions (not shown). This map allows seeing how conservation priorities are relocated as the relative cost of productive areas increases.

For better visualization, it is recommended to use the browser’s full-screen mode. The viewer is designed for optimal display in Full HD (1920x1080). The activation of classes is carried out in groups. 7.2 Right Panel The right panel has two tabs: one for data analysis and another for a description of the selected prioritization map. The data analysis tab has two modes: data analysis for prioritization maps, described in Sec. 7.2.1, and interaction analysis with productive areas, described in Sec. 7.2.2. 7.2.1 Prioritization Data Analysis Figure 7.4: For prioritization maps, the right panel displays a slider that allows selecting the percentage of area dedicated to conservation, ranging from 10% (current protected areas) to 30% (including the four priority levels). Additionally, two charts showing target fulfillment are displayed. The prioritization maps, in the 9 available analysis variants, activate the data analysis controls in the right-hand panel. The slider at the top allows you to select the amount of priority area to be displayed (see Fig. 7.4). The possible values range from 10%, in which case only the protected areas are displayed (if that reference layer is selected, see Sec. 7.1.2). The slider allows you to add priority levels one by one, starting from the highest in sequential order. Each level represents 5% of the territory, up to a maximum of 30%. As the slider moves, a gray dashed vertical line indicates the level of target achievement for each conservation feature, as shown in Fig. 7.5). The graph below shows the average target achievement for the different animal classes considered. Figure 7.5: The graphs show how the target fulfillment increases as more land is dedicated to conservation. The top graph shows the progress of biodiversity (green), water (blue), carbon (brown) and the average of them (black). The progress of prioritizing joint targets is also shown in dashed lines. This represents the maximum achievable value. 7.2.2 Analysis of Interaction with Productive Areas The right-hand panel has a special configuration for the case of interaction with productive areas. In this case, the top slider controls the relative cost of productive areas, as shown in Fig. 7.6. As this value increases, the level of interaction between the prioritization solutions and production areas decreases. In these cases, the prioritization of joint targets (biodiversity, carbon, and water) is considered, using 30% of the surface. For more information on the model and the meaning of the relative cost, see Sec. 5.5. Figure 7.6: For the analysis of interaction with productive areas, the right-hand panel includes a slider to control the level of interaction through the relative cost of productive areas. As this value increases, the prioritization result changes. Below the main relative cost slider is the control for layers of interaction with productive areas, along with its corresponding opacity control. The available options, which are mutually exclusive, are: Priority levels only: Only the result of the modified joint target prioritization (Sec. 5.5) is shown, including the 4 priority levels and varying the relative cost of productive areas (Fig. 7.6). Overlap: A layer is activated that overlaps with the previous one, showing the high-priority conservation areas that spatially coincide with agricultural, livestock, or forestry production areas (see Fig. 7.7). Difference with the original solution: A layer is activated that overlaps with the priority areas, showing the areas that become more prioritized (red) and those that should be removed from the original solution to reduce the interaction of the conservation solution with production areas. Figure 7.7: The overlap of each conservation solution with production coverages is visualized in orange tones according to the level of coincidence in each PU (three levels are considered). The total overlap value, relative to the total productive area, can be seen on the x-axis of the graph, indicated by a vertical line. Figure 7.8: The third option for the layers of interaction with productive areas is the difference with the original solution. In red, the areas of the new solution that are not in the original solution are shown, and in blue, the areas of the original solution that are not in the solution with reduced interaction. This map shows how priority areas need to be relocated to maintain a high level of target fulfillment while reducing spatial overlap with food and forestry production regions. The graph shows the level of target fulfillment for biodiversity, carbon, water, and their average as a function of overlap with productive areas. The original solution is located on the far right, with an overlap of about 15% of the approximately 53 million hectares dedicated to food or forestry production. As a higher relative cost is introduced into the model for productive areas, the optimization process progressively selects fewer productive areas. The strength of the algorithm developed in this work is its ability to maintain a high level of target fulfillment while reducing overlap with productive areas. Initially, the level of biodiversity protection remains almost constant, water protection decreases, and biomass carbon protection increases, showing a synergistic behavior for this conservation feature.

8 Visualization Tools 8.1 Zoom Buttons 8.2 Reset View 8.3 Background Layers 8.4 Drawing Tools 8.5 Measurement Tool 8.6 Print

8 Visualization Tools The visualization tools are located on the main window. Their purpose is to achieve precision and detail in the observation and data collection within the viewer. There are zoom tools (8.1 and 8.2), background layer controls (8.3), drawing tools (8.4), topographic tools for measuring distances, surfaces, and perimeters (8.5). Additionally, this tool displays geographic information about the location of interest. Finally, there is a print button (8.6). Figure 8.1: Visualization tools. 8.1 Zoom Buttons The zoom tools allow you to adjust the scale of the main window. You can use the zoom buttons for greater precision or the mouse wheel for faster adjustments. 8.2 Reset View This button restores the image to its initial scale and centers the map in the main window. 8.3 Background Layers The viewer starts with a white and gray background map, on which the prioritization maps stand out. However, it is possible to activate different background layer modes. You can select the satellite mode to view different environments in general, the road and path mode, and the topographic mode to observe relief differences (Fig. 8.2). Figure 8.2: By default, the viewer starts with a white and gray background map to highlight the prioritization maps, but it is also possible to activate satellite images, road and path maps, and topographic maps with relief. 8.4 Drawing Tools The drawing tools allow you to create polygons manually or using predefined shapes, create lines and polylines, use site indicators, and save this information. When they are used, a secondary menu for start and end points is displayed (Fig. 8.3). To draw the figures, click and drag the pointer. The vertices are editable. It is recommended to draw continuously to avoid overlaps and vertex crossings in the figures. Figure 8.3: Drawing tools for lines, geometric shapes, and markers. 8.5 Measurement Tool The measurement tools allow you to measure distances and areas. These can be position markers (fixed points), straight-line distances, or freehand-drawn figures. The result shows the georeferencing of the point (position marker) or the location of the last fixed point if it is a figure. When using the tool, a submenu is displayed where you can mark the start and end of the measurement, and then the result is shown. These figures allow you to measure surfaces and distances directly from the viewer’s products. You can measure coverages and overlaps of results, obtaining instant data on areas and distances according to the goals chosen in each map (see Fig. 8.4). This measurement tool can be combined with the drawing tools, by creating the figure first or placing one or more position markers and then performing the measurements. Figure 8.4: The measurement tool allows you to obtain distances, areas, and perimeters. 8.6 Print Finally, the working map can be saved as an image in A4 size (portrait or landscape) using the button located at the bottom left of the visualization area.
